I am a 48-year-old farmer in Quzhou County with four years of experience working this land. My family has four people to feed, and I have 200 mu and a well for irrigation. Out here on the North China Plain, the wheat-maize double crop is the backbone of everything. My winter wheat went into the ground last October, so right now it is greening up and my main job is spring management. I will topdress nitrogen at reviving and again at jointing, irrigate four times through grain filling, and spray three times for aphids and powdery mildew. I use improved wheat varieties because they resist lodging and give steady yields.

Come early June, right after wheat harvest, I have a narrow window to plant summer maize. I plant hybrid seed directly into the wheat stubble with no-tillage — there is no time to plow, and the straw helps hold moisture. I fertilize at planting, topdress at the big-flare stage, irrigate three times, and spray two or three times depending on corn borer pressure.

I keep 25 mu for spring cabbage. It is labor-heavy but the early crop fetches a good price at market. I plant hybrid varieties, give it heavy fertilizer and five irrigations, and spray four times because caterpillars are relentless.

The remaining 15 mu I put into stevia. A buyer from Shandong purchases dried leaves at a price better than grain, so it is worth the risk. Stevia is fussy — it needs steady water, careful weeding, and moderate fertilizer with enough potassium. I plant improved seedlings, irrigate four times, spray twice, and harvest twice over summer and autumn.

This mix keeps my family fed, covers costs through grain sales, and gives me extra cash from the vegetables and specialty crop.
